This REIT Has 10.4% Yield and Low Gearing: How Strong Is Its Income Case?
article:
At 62 Singapore cents, Sasseur REIT offers a
10.4%
trailing distribution yield.
The calculation uses 6.449 cents per unit distributed for 2H2025 and 1H2026.
The combination of a 10.4% trailing yield, 25.3% gearing,
6.8 times
interest coverage and cheaper debt makes Sasseur worth a closer look for income investors.

Weighted average borrowing costs fell to 3.6% at end-Sept, from 4.4% at end-2025.

All borrowings are denominated in renminbi, with the sponsor providing half.
CFO Ella Jia explained that “previously, the onshore loan was actually LPR plus, and with this refinancing it is actually LPR minus”.
This means the new loan is priced below China’s Loan Prime Rate (LPR).

Retail performance was less buoyant

Retail performance was less buoyant

Sasseur's 12 Nov briefing highlighted high occupancy, alongside softer retail spending.
Nine-month outlet sales rose 4.4% to RMB3.39 billion, but third-quarter sales fell 2%.
3Q2026 average occupancy nevertheless improved to 98.6% from 97.2% in the preceding quarter.
The anniversary promotions started later in September and extended into October.

Sasseur's 12 Nov briefing highlighted high occupancy, alongside softer retail spending.

Management said outlet sales from July to 7 October grew slightly year on year.

The renewal that matters

Sasseur’s entrusted management agreement (EMA) cushion its rental income through a fixed component that rises 3% annually, alongside a variable component linked to outlet sales.
Fixed rent contributed about 71% of nine-month EMA rental income, providing a substantial buffer against fluctuations in tenant sales.

That structure helped nine-month rental income grow 3.4% in renminbi.
A stronger Chinese currency lifted the increase to 6.9% in Singapore dollars, reaching S$97.6 million.

The current agreements expire in March 2028.
CEO Cheng Hsing Yuen
called the EMA “a foundational pillar of our Sasseur REIT value proposition”, with renewal discussions under way.
He stressed:

CEO Cheng Hsing Yuen

He stressed:

“Our priority is to ensure that the renewed EMA framework is as robust and watertight as possible to safeguard the distribution and protect the long-term interests of our unitholders.”

Management is reviewing operational parameters against current market conditions; it has not disclosed an agreed replacement contract or announcement timetable.

Understanding the manager’s unit sales

Asked about the manager’s sale of 25 million units across August and September, the CEO gave some context.

Cheng said institutional investors and high-net-worth individuals had approached Sasseur because they wanted to invest.
He emphasised that the interest came from them:

“They reached out to us—not that we reached out to them. They came to us and said they wanted to invest.”

He said these investors had shown keen interest in Sasseur REIT’s platform and outlet business model.

The five transactions by
Sasseur Asset Management generated gross proceeds of S$16.85 million for the manager
.

Sasseur Asset Management generated gross proceeds of S$16.85 million for the manager

It receives part of its management fees in REIT units: for the first half of 2026, 60% of the base fee was paid this way. The remaining 40% was paid in cash by the REIT.

These fees are the manager’s business income, supporting staff salaries and other overheads. Selling units converts that fee income into cash.

An income opportunity with conditions

Sasseur’s lower financing costs and high occupancy support its income appeal.
Sasseur head of investor relations & capital markets
Its yield is attractive, but its sustainability depends on rental durability, consumer spending and currency movements.

The main uncertainty is the revised rental framework and its terms -- particularly the fixed rental component, annual escalation and duration of any extension --
after March 2028.

title: How to Balance REIT Dividends with US Growth Stocks for Maximum Returns
article:
Ask the people around you how they want to grow their wealth, and the answer is usually one of two things: steady dividends or capital appreciation.
And the go-to is usually Singapore real estate investment trusts (S-REITs) for the former and US tech giants for the latter.
However, going all-in on either means taking on all of its weak spots.
When you mix REITs with
US growth stocks
, you strike a balance between consistent cash flow and long-term upside.
Here’s how to make them work together.
Why Combine REITs and US Growth Stocks?
REITs own
income-generating properties
like malls and warehouses, collect rent, and pay out 90%+ of taxable income for corporate tax breaks.
That high payout makes them an income favourite.
Reinvest the payout, and watch your money snowball faster.
On the flip side, big tech stalwarts like
Microsoft Corporation
(NASDAQ: MSFT),
Alphabet Inc
(NASDAQ: GOOGL), and
Amazon.com Inc
(NASDAQ: AMZN) skip the hefty payouts and pour their cash directly into expansion, especially AI and cloud infrastructure.
They run on entirely different engines.
Blending them gives you sensible diversification, but don’t treat it like a bulletproof hedge.
When a sharp sell-off strikes, both can easily drop at the same time.
Choosing the Right Singapore REITs for Dividend Income
A fat yield means little if the payout behind it is shrinking.
So before buying a REIT, always check if its payout is growing.
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U), Singapore’s largest REIT, raised its distribution per unit (DPU) by 7.1% to S$0.0602 in 1H2026.
This was driven by strong rental reversions of 4.0% in retail and 6.5% in offices, alongside a resilient occupancy rate of 95.6%.
In contrast,
Mapletree Industrial Trust
(SGX: ME8U)’s 1HFY2026/2027 DPU slipped 5.7% to S$0.0608 after property sales and weaker occupancy at its North American portfolio.
A headline yield above 6% is definitely juicy, but a declining payout quickly erodes that initial appeal.
Balance sheet strength also plays a critical role.
When interest rates stay elevated, a REIT’s gearing directly impacts the bottom line.
CICT maintains a gearing ratio of 37.4% with an average cost of debt at 2.9%.
Healthcare pure-play
Parkway Life REIT
(SGX: C2PU) runs even leaner at 33.8% gearing, helping power a 14.6% jump in its 1H2026 DPU on the back of rising Singapore hospital rents.
That’s why sector diversification matters too!
Malls, offices, hospitals, and warehouses all answer to different tenants, so a slump in one won’t sink your payouts.
Selecting US Growth Stocks for Long-Term Capital Appreciation
For a growth company to stay great, it needs something special, something rivals find hard to copy.
Companies like Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon have that kind of edge.
Microsoft reported 19.0% year-on-year (YoY) growth in revenue to US$92.3 billion for 1QFY2027, with its Azure cloud business up 48.0%.
Alphabet’s 3Q2026 revenue climbed 25.0% YoY to US$127.6 billion as Google Cloud revenue soared 103.0%.
Similarly, Amazon posted 12.0% YoY growth to US$201.9 billion for 3Q2026, as AWS sales were up 39.0%.
However, growth only counts if it eventually becomes free cash flow.
And here’s where the picture splits.
Over the past 12 months, Microsoft generated US$60.0 billion of free cash flow and Alphabet US$19.4 billion, although Alphabet’s quarterly free cash flow has dipped below zero in each of the last two quarters.
Meanwhile, Amazon swung to a negative US$42.4 billion as its AI spending ballooned.
That said, negative cash flow is not necessarily bad if those data centres pay off, but it is still a risk to watch.
How Much Should You Allocate to REITs vs US Growth Stocks?
There’s no perfect asset split for everyone.
It simply comes down to your age, goals, and how many ups and downs you can stomach.
If you’re close to retiring, locking in consistent cash flow and capital preservation takes priority.
But if you have decades ahead, you can ride out bigger swings for more growth.
Here is a hypothetical S$100,000 split.

S-REITs
US Growth Stocks

Assumes average distribution yields of 5.45% for S-REIT and dividend yields of 0.35% for US growth stocks.
The income-focused mix pays the most today and swings the least, but grows more slowly.
The growth-focused mix pays little now but has the most upside, and bumpiest ride.
Remember, this two-asset combo is just a baseline model, not a complete portfolio.
You’ll still want an emergency cash cushion, some bond allocation for ballast, and broad-market shares outside of property and tech.
How Dividends and Growth Can Work Together
While you are building wealth, reinvest your REIT distributions into more units, or into
growth stocks
when their valuations look reasonable.
That helps rebalance your portfolio without selling anything.
As retirement nears, gradually shift towards income.
Let your stage of life drive the change and not the latest headlines.
What Are the Risks of Combining REITs and US Growth Stocks?
Interest rates are one of the most important risks to watch, as they cut both ways.
Higher rates raise REIT borrowing costs and tend to drag down growth-stock prices too.
Currency is another.
As US stocks are priced in US dollars, if the greenback weakens against the Singapore dollar, your returns shrink when converted back.
Also, watch out for concentration.
Having three technology giants or five shopping malls is not diversification.
Lastly, volatility.
Both can drop 20% or more, so keep an emergency fund and you’ll never be forced to sell at the bottom.
How to Measure Whether Your Portfolio Is Working
Watch your total return – payouts plus price changes.
A 7% yielder whose unit price falls 10% has still lost you money.
Check that your REITs’ DPU rises over time and review your portfolio at least once a year.
If your mix drifts off target, rebalance based on business fundamentals, not price swings.
Get Smart: Balance Income Today with Growth Tomorrow
REITs pay you now while growth stocks build wealth for later.
Whatever the mix, judge each holding on payout quality, debt, and cash flow, not just its yield.
That goal is never to buy the biggest yield or hottest stock.
It’s simply to
build a portfolio
that delivers solid total returns and fits your life.
Not all AI “winners” will survive this cycle.
But a few companies already have the scale, cash flow, and edge to pull ahead. We highlight what to look for in our FREE volatile market report.

title: World leaders at Manila summit seek trade to offset US risks
article:
(Nov 16) : Several world leaders converge on the Philippines this week for a regional summit, with many seeking to deepen trade links as a hedge against the rising US protectionism under President Donald Trump.

Canada’s Mark Carney, Brazil’s Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Australia’s Anthony Albanese were in attendance Sunday at the kickoff of the three-day Association of Southeast Asian Nations leaders’ summit, with trade and regional security matters the focus of discussions. Chinese Premier Li Qiang arrived late Sunday, while India’s Narendra Modi and Japan’s Sanae Takaichi are expected in coming days.

Trump will make an appearance in Manila as well, but only late Tuesday afternoon as the summit is concluding. He’ll be in the country less than 24 hours before flying to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, where he’ll participate in a highly anticipated trilateral summit with China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.

The diplomatic push in Manila underscores a broader scramble by middle power countries like Canada, Brazil, Australia and European nations to diversify their trade and defense partnerships. The Trump administration’s heavy tariffs and a prolonged conflict in Iran has strained trade relations and global energy supply chains.

That momentum was visible Sunday as Carney unveiled new trade pacts with the Philippines and the 11-member Asean group. Meanwhile, Carney and Lula signaled deepening ties with each other, pledging millions of dollars to protect tropical forests and planning reciprocal state visits.

Elsewhere on the sidelines, Australia and the Philippines inked a new defense pact to bolster regional security, while French President Emmanuel Macron is set to secure several bilateral agreements, including on trade, during a separate conference in Cambodia over the weekend.

See also: US logs US$404 billion deficit in first month of fiscal year

In his address to leaders on Sunday, Lula called for stronger cooperation among countries and respect for multilateralism. In the face of Trump’s high tariffs, “instead of weeping or begging the US government,” Brazil was better off finding new partners to plug any trade gaps, Lula told reporters in Manila.

Top of mind for Southeast Asian nations during Trump’s visit will be addressing anxieties over potential US export controls on chips to choke off supplies to China. The exit of Nvidia Corp.’s Jensen Huang after his affair with an alleged Chinese spy exposed the possible illicit trade of US-restricted chips from Southeast Asian nations. Tighter rules on exports of the chips could slow the AI-fueled economic boom in countries like Malaysia and Singapore.

With the region becoming an increasingly vital hub for data centers and semiconductor manufacturing, the Asean bloc over the weekend signed a landmark Digital Economy Framework Agreement covering among other things, cybersecurity, AI, and cross-border data sharing.

See also: Stocks fall on Nvidia rout as oil jump sinks bonds

At the previous leaders’ meeting “we discussed how the world has become more contested and unpredictable,” Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong told his counterparts on Sunday. “Unfortunately, the situation has continued to remain highly volatile.”

On regional security matters, the South China Sea is a focus area, especially for the Philippines, which has over the years clashed repeatedly with China in waters where they have competing territorial claims.

Asean leaders said Sunday they reached a “substantial completion of the negotiations” with China on a Code of Conduct in the South China Sea and expect to have it completed by next year.
